blocks.prompt: The House You Carry on Your Back
blocks.text: A tent is a home you can carry. The word tent comes from an old word that means to stretch. That is just what a tent does. Poles push up. Pegs pull down. The cloth is pulled tight in between. Tight cloth sheds rain. Loose cloth sags, and water sits in the sag until it drips through. People have slept in tents for thousands of years. Some families still live in them all year. When it is time to move, they fold the tent, load it up, and set it up again somewhere new.

blocks.prompt: The Oldest Building We Still Use
blocks.text: A tent is the oldest kind of building people still use. The word comes from the Latin word tendere, which means to stretch, and stretching is the whole secret. The poles push up. The pegs and ropes pull down and out. The cloth in between is pulled so tight that rain slides off instead of soaking in. Roman soldiers marched with tents made of goat leather. Eight soldiers shared one tent, and they carried it in pieces on a mule. On the plains of North America, families built tall cone shaped tipis from poles and hides, with flaps at the top that could be opened to let smoke out. In the deserts of Arabia, people wove tents from black goat hair. The weave is loose, so air moves through on hot days. When rain comes, the hair swells and closes the gaps, and the tent turns into a roof. Every one of those tents does the same three jobs. It keeps the weather out. It comes apart. It goes back up somewhere else.

notes: Poles are in compression, ropes are in tension

blocks.prompt: A Machine for Handling Forces
blocks.text: Look closely at a tent and you are looking at a machine for handling forces. The poles are in compression, which means they are being squeezed. The fabric and the guy ropes are in tension, which means they are being pulled. Nothing is holding the tent up by being heavy. It stands because the pushing and the pulling are balanced against each other. Loosen one guy rope and the balance breaks. The wall goes slack, the wind gets a grip on the loose cloth, and the whole thing shakes. The old army tents were ridge tents: a straight pole at each end and a bar across the top, like a house roof with the walls removed. They were steady, but they were also heavy, and the sloping walls wasted space inside. In the 1970s campers started using dome tents instead. A dome tent has flexible poles that arch over the top and cross each other. Each pole is bent, and a bent pole is always trying to spring straight, which pushes outward against the fabric and keeps the whole shape tight. That is why a dome tent stands up on its own before you have hammered in a single peg. Modern tents usually have two layers. The inner layer is thin and breathable. The outer layer, called the rainfly, is coated to be waterproof. The gap between them matters more than it looks. A sleeping person breathes out water vapor all night. If there is only one layer, that vapor hits the cold waterproof wall, turns back into drops, and rains on you from the inside.

answers: compression is being squeezed (the poles); tension is being pulled (the fabric and ropes)

(inference: the tent stands on balanced forces, so one slack side lets wind grip the loose cloth)

blocks.prompt: The Building With Nothing Holding It Down
blocks.text: A tent is a building with no walls to speak of, no foundation, and no weight to hold it down, and yet a good one can survive a storm that flattens a fence. It manages this by turning every force that hits it into something the structure can pass along. The poles carry compression, squeezed from both ends. The fabric and the guy lines carry tension, pulled tight in every direction. Wind pushing on one side of a tent is answered by a rope and a peg on the other. The shape matters more than the strength of any single part: curves and triangles spread a load, while flat panels catch it. Different climates produced different answers. In the deserts of Arabia and North Africa, the Bedouin wove tents from black goat hair, a fabric that looks like the worst possible choice for a hot place. It works. The dark cloth is loosely woven, so a breeze passes through it while the sun does not, and the heat rising under the roof pulls more air in behind it. When rain finally arrives, the goat hair fibers swell, the gaps close, and the same cloth becomes a roof. On the grasslands of North America, Plains nations built tipis, cones of poles and hide with adjustable smoke flaps at the top that let a family keep a fire burning indoors. In Central Asia, the Mongolian ger uses a lattice wall of wood and thick felt made from sheep wool, warm enough for winters that drop far below freezing, and light enough to be taken down and moved. The strangest survivor is the pyramid tent used in Antarctica. Its design dates back to the British expeditions of the early 1900s, four poles meeting at a point with the fabric stretched between them, and it is still pitched on the ice today. Newer designs come and go. This one stays because a pyramid has no flat face for the wind to push against, from any direction, and in a place where a storm can last a week, that is worth more than being clever.

blocks.prompt: An Argument With Gravity: How a Tent Stands Up
blocks.text: Almost every building humans make is an argument with gravity. Stone, brick, and timber all work the same way: pile heavy things on top of heavier things and let weight hold the structure in place. A tent argues differently. It has no weight worth mentioning and no foundation at all, and it stays standing by keeping opposite forces in a permanent standoff. The poles are in compression, squeezed along their length. The fabric and the guy lines are in tension, pulled tight in every direction at once. Remove either side of that bargain and the tent is a bag of cloth again. That principle is ancient, and the word itself records it. Tent comes from the Latin tendere, to stretch. Stretch is the operative verb. A taut surface sheds water and sheds wind. A slack surface collects rain in its sagging middle and offers the wind a loose edge to work at, and wind, given an edge, will always find a way in. Because the physics is simple, the interesting variation is cultural. In the deserts of Arabia and North Africa, Bedouin families wove their tents from black goat hair, which sounds like the worst material available in a place defined by sun. It is close to ideal. The weave is deliberately open, so a breeze passes through the cloth while the sun does not, and hot air escaping upward drags cooler air in behind it. When rain does come, the fibers absorb water and swell, the gaps between them shut, and a curtain becomes a roof. On the North American plains, tipis solved a different problem: keeping a fire indoors. Two adjustable flaps at the apex could be angled with outside poles as the wind shifted, drawing smoke up and out instead of into the family's lungs. In Central Asia, the Mongolian ger answered brutal cold with a collapsible wooden lattice and heavy felt pressed from sheep wool, a structure warm enough for a winter camp and light enough to be loaded onto animals when the grass ran out. Militaries drove the engineering. Roman legions carried tents of stitched goat leather, one shared between the eight soldiers of a contubernium, which meant a tent had to be light enough to be split up and packed onto a mule. Ridge tents, two upright poles and a horizontal bar, remained the standard for centuries because they were simple to make and simple to repair. They were also heavy, and their sloping walls wasted most of the space inside. The modern dome tent, which arrived with campers in the 1970s, throws the ridge out entirely. Its poles are flexible and are threaded through sleeves so that they arch and cross overhead. Each one is bent, and a bent pole never stops trying to straighten, so it presses outward against the fabric and holds the whole shell taut from within. The structure is stable before a single peg goes in, and there are no vertical walls to catch a gust. One old design refuses to be improved. The pyramid tent taken to Antarctica by British expeditions in the early 1900s is, in its essentials, the tent still pitched on the ice today. Four poles meeting at a point, fabric stretched between them, no flat face for wind to shove against from any angle. Newer shapes are lighter and pack smaller. In a place where a storm may last a week, nobody has been willing to bet a life on lighter.
